paragraphs: Welcome to the night shift. You're the only analyst on until 6 AM.
Kestrel employees forward anything that looks off to the SOC inbox. Your job is to decide on each one: Report it as phishing, or Trust it as legitimate.

Don't take anything at face value. Hover over the sender to see the real address. Hover over links to see where they really go. Check attachment names closely. On a touch screen, tap instead of hovering.
When something looks wrong, click it to flag it (on a touch screen, tap it a second time). A correct flag earns XP, but a wrong one costs you, so don't just click everything.
The clock moves forward each time you close out an email. Make it to 6 AM.

emails.forwardNote: Diane never texts me like this. Can you check before I buy anything?
emails.subject: Quick favor, need gift cards ASAP
body: Tyler,
Are you at your desk? I need a quick favor.
I'm in back-to-back meetings with a client and can't take calls.

body.text: Please buy five $200 gift cards for client appreciation and send me photos of the card numbers.
I need them within the hour.
Keep this between us for now, I want it to be a surprise.

body: I'll reimburse you tomorrow.
Diane
Sent from my phone

redFlags.sender: The display name says Diane Okafor, but the address is a personal Gmail account. Executives use their company address for company business.
redFlags.giftcards: Gift cards are a classic scam payment. Once someone has the card numbers, the money is gone and can't be traced.
redFlags.urgency: "Within the hour" creates pressure so you act before you think or check with anyone.
redFlags.secrecy: Asking you to keep it quiet stops you from checking with a coworker who would spot the scam.

emails.explanation: This is CEO fraud, a kind of business email compromise. The attacker pretends to be an executive and uses authority, urgency, and secrecy to rush an employee into sending money. Check by calling the executive on a number you already know, not by replying.

emails.forwardNote: We get carrier notices all day, but I don't recognize this one.
emails.subject: Delivery failed: see invoice

body.text: Dear Customer,

body: We were unable to deliver your package (tracking #FL-30471-88) because of an unpaid customs fee.
Please open the attached invoice and pay the balance to schedule redelivery.

body.text: If payment is not received within 48 hours, your package will be returned to sender.

body: FreightLine Customer Care

redFlags.attachment: The real file name is Invoice_8841.pdf.exe. The ".pdf" is fake. It's a program that runs when opened, most likely malware. Windows hides known extensions by default, which is why this trick works.
redFlags.sender: Kestrel doesn't use a carrier called FreightLine, and the domain is a long, made-up "alerts" domain, not a carrier's real site.
redFlags.greeting: "Dear Customer" means the sender doesn't know who you are. A real carrier would name the account or shipper.
redFlags.urgency: A 48-hour deadline plus a surprise fee is pressure to open the attachment without checking.

emails.explanation: This is a malware delivery email. A fake shipping notice is a believable lure at a logistics company. The double extension (.pdf.exe) is the giveaway: always check the full file name, and never open an executable attachment from an email.

emails.forwardNote: Looks like it's from IT. Should I click it? I really can't lose dispatch access tonight.
emails.subject: Your password expires in 24 hours
body: Hello Jordan,

body.text: Our records show your network password expires in 24 hours.
To keep your current password and avoid losing access to email and the dispatch system, confirm your account using the button below.
Keep My Current Password

body: Thank you,
Kestrel IT Service Desk

redFlags.sender: Look closely: kestre1-logistics.com uses the number 1 in place of the letter l. This is a lookalike domain made to pass a quick glance.
redFlags.link: The button text looks harmless, but the link goes to verify-acct.net, not a Kestrel site. That's a credential harvesting page.
redFlags.urgency: A 24-hour countdown pushes you to act before you check.
redFlags.keep: Real IT password policies make you change an expiring password, not keep it. Offering to "keep your current password" is bait to get it typed into a fake page.

emails.explanation: This is credential phishing with a lookalike (typosquatted) domain. Read sender domains letter by letter, hover every link before clicking, and change your password only through the company's own portal, never through an email link.

emails.forwardNote: Meeting moved with no warning. Is this real?
emails.subject: Team sync moved to Thursday
body: Hi team,
Wednesday's fleet ops sync conflicts with the quarterly safety audit, so I've moved it to Thursday at 10:00 AM in Conference Room B.
Same agenda as before.
Please bring your route utilization numbers for October.
Thanks,
Sam
emails.explanation: This one is legitimate. It comes from a real kestrel-logistics.com address, gives a clear business reason for the change, has no links or attachments, and asks for nothing sensitive. A surprise schedule change is not a red flag by itself. Reporting every real email wastes the team's time and wears down trust in the SOC.

emails.forwardNote: I don't know who shared this. It mentions salaries, so I didn't want to ignore it.
emails.subject: A document was shared with you

body.text: Dear user,
A document has been shared with you: Q4_Salary_Adjustments.xlsx

body: Click below to view the document.

body.text: You will need to sign in with your email password to open it.
Open Document

body: This link will expire in 12 hours.
FileHarbor Sharing Service

redFlags.greeting: "Dear user" is generic. A real share notice names the person who shared the file with you.
redFlags.sender: Kestrel doesn't use a file-sharing service called FileHarbor, and no coworker's name appears anywhere in the message.
redFlags.lure: A salary spreadsheet is bait. It plays on curiosity, especially for someone in HR.
redFlags.creds: Asking for your email password to open a shared file is a credential grab. Company files open through your normal single sign-on.
redFlags.link: The link uses plain http:// (no encryption) and goes to secure-docview.co, an unknown domain that has nothing to do with the sender.

emails.explanation: This is credential phishing disguised as a file-share notice. No named sharer, a generic greeting, a curiosity lure, and an unencrypted link to an unrelated domain add up to a fake login page. Report it and check with the supposed sharer some other way.

emails.forwardNote: Every holiday email this season has been a scam of some kind. Is this one real before I start planning around it?
emails.subject: Updated 2027 holiday schedule
body: Hello Kestrel team,
The 2027 company holiday schedule is now final.
We updated it after last month's feedback, so Independence Day and Christmas now land on the weekday closest to the holiday.

Office holidays for 2027: New Year's Day (Fri, Jan 1), Memorial Day (Mon, May 31), Independence Day (observed Mon, Jul 5), Labor Day (Mon, Sep 6), Thanksgiving (Thu and Fri, Nov 25 and 26), and Christmas (observed Fri, Dec 24).
Warehouse, dispatch, and fleet teams keep running on holidays.
If you work a company holiday, you earn holiday pay at 1.5 times your rate. Shift swaps go through your supervisor as usual.
The full calendar, including floating holidays, is on the intranet:

body.text: 2027 Holiday Calendar

body: Thanks,
Kestrel People Team
emails.explanation: This one is legitimate. It comes from the real HR address on kestrel-logistics.com, the dates are specific and check out against a calendar, it asks for nothing, and the only link goes to the company's own intranet. Holiday emails are a popular phishing lure this time of year, so being careful was reasonable. But a lure that's in season doesn't make every email about it fake: check the sender and the link, and if they're clean, trust it.

emails.forwardNote: I never touched my bank info. Is someone stealing my paycheck? Should I log in and cancel it?
emails.subject: Direct deposit change confirmed

body.text: Dear Employee,
This message confirms that the direct deposit account on your payroll profile was changed today.

body: Your next paycheck will be sent to the new account ending in 4471.

body.text: If you did not make this change, you must cancel it within 6 hours or your December 4 paycheck will be deposited to the new account.
Log in to cancel this change

body: Kestrel Payroll Services
This is an automated message. Do not reply.

redFlags.unrequested: It "confirms" a change Marcus never made. The scare is the hook: the attacker wants him to panic and log in to undo it.
redFlags.link: The "cancel" link goes to paycenter-employee-login.net, not a Kestrel site. Logging in there hands over the password that controls his paycheck.
redFlags.sender: The address is kestrel-payrollcenter.com, a lookalike domain that only contains the company name. Real payroll mail comes from kestrel-logistics.com.
redFlags.greeting: "Dear Employee" is generic. A real payroll notice is addressed to you by name.
redFlags.urgency: A 6-hour deadline tied to your paycheck pushes you to click before you think to call payroll.

emails.explanation: This is credential phishing aimed at payroll, a common setup for direct deposit fraud. A message about a change you never made is meant to make you act out of fear. Never use the email's own link to "fix" a problem: go to the payroll portal through the intranet yourself, or call HR on a number you already know.

emails.forwardNote: We got a fake IT email last month, so now I don't trust anything from IT. Do I need to do something before 2 AM?
emails.subject: Scheduled maintenance tonight at 2 AM
body: Hi night shift,
Tonight from 2:00 to 2:30 AM, we're installing security updates on the email servers.
During that window, email on desktops and phones may be slow or unavailable.
The dispatch system, warehouse scanners, and fleet tracking are not affected and will keep running normally.
There's nothing you need to do.
You don't need to log out, restart, or install anything. Email will reconnect on its own when the work is done.
If something still isn't working after 2:30 AM, call the IT Service Desk at extension 4400.
Thanks for your patience,
Priya Natarajan
IT Operations, Kestrel Logistics
emails.explanation: This one is legitimate. It comes from the real IT address on kestrel-logistics.com, it's signed by a named person, it has no links or attachments, and it asks for nothing. It even tells you to call the Service Desk's internal extension if there's a problem, which is how real IT works. Compare it to the fake password email earlier tonight: that one wanted you to click and sign in. This one just tells you what's happening.

emails.forwardNote: Harbor Point is one of our regular fuel vendors and the invoice number matches. I'm queuing payments for the morning run. Okay to update their bank info?

from.name: Linda Marsh, Harbor Point Fuel Supply

emails.subject: Updated bank details for invoice #2291
body: Hi Grace,
Hope the holiday week is treating you well.
Quick update on our end: after an audit, Harbor Point has moved its business banking.

body.text: Please send payment for invoice #2291 ($48,612.50) to our new account, routing 091407752, account ending 7720, instead of the account you have on file.
The invoice is due Friday, so please update it in this morning's payment run to avoid a late fee.
Our office phones are being moved to a new provider this week, so please just reply to this email to confirm the change.

body: Thank you!
Linda Marsh
Accounts Receivable, Harbor Point Fuel Supply

redFlags.replyTo: The From address is Harbor Point's real domain, but replies go to harborpoint-fuel.co, a different domain. Whoever reads those replies is not Harbor Point.
redFlags.newaccount: A request to send a large payment to a brand-new bank account is the core of the scam. Bank changes should always be confirmed by phone with a contact you already have on file.
redFlags.nocall: "Just reply to this email" steers you away from calling the vendor, which is the one check that would expose the fraud.
redFlags.urgency: A due date and a late fee push AP to change the account in tonight's run, before anyone has time to call.

emails.explanation: This is vendor email compromise, a kind of business email compromise. The attacker either broke into the vendor's real mailbox or spoofed it, so the From line looks right and the invoice number is real. The clues are the mismatched Reply-To, a new bank account, and a reason not to call. The PDF looks normal and is just a real PDF: a clean attachment doesn't make an email safe. Always confirm bank changes by calling the vendor on a number you already have, never one from the email.

emails.forwardNote: An email about phishing, with a link in it? Feels like exactly the kind of trap the training would warn us about.
emails.subject: Phishing awareness training due Friday
body: Hi everyone,
Our yearly phishing awareness training is due by Friday, December 4.
It takes about 20 minutes and covers lookalike domains, fake invoices, and what to do with a suspicious email.
Open it from the Training page on the intranet, the same way you reach your other required courses:

body.text: Phishing Awareness 2026

body: You'll sign in with your normal company login, like any other intranet page.
As a reminder, the Security team will never ask for your password by email or phone.
If something in your inbox looks off, forward it to the SOC. That's what we're here for.
Thanks,
Kestrel Security Team
emails.explanation: This one is legitimate. It comes from the real security team address on kestrel-logistics.com, the link goes to the company intranet, and the due date is a week away, not a few hours. It asks you to sign in through your normal company login, not to type a password into some outside page. An email about phishing isn't phishing just because of its topic. Judge it by the same checks as everything else: sender, links, and what it asks you to do.
